clue.text: Grab an unreasonable amount, it is noised abroad

indicators.note: something noised is spread by word of mouth, so the phrase before is heard spoken, not read

parts.note: to seize too much is to over-seize

explanation.surface: Someone's greedy grab becomes rumour spreading far and wide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noised abroad' reads as one idiom for rumour, but 'abroad' alone is the definition and 'it is noised' signals the sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe being in foreign lands, across the sea from home.

clue.text: Without fish to sell, I left, needing to be elsewhere

indicators.note: left here means departed, so the letter I walks out of the phrase

parts.note: a fishmonger without stock is out of plaice, plaice being a flatfish

explanation.surface: A fishmonger with nothing to sell walks out, wishing to be somewhere else.
explanation.walkthrough: PLAICE is a common British flatfish; losing its I turns it into PLACE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something misplaced is not where it belongs, so it ought to be moved somewhere else.

clue.text: Big beast of somewhat novel kind

indicators.note: only somewhat of the words is used, a run of letters taken from inside them

explanation.surface: A large animal of an unusual sort.
explanation.definitionFit: The elk is a very large deer, certainly a big beast.

clue.text: From unknown, note included in flowers sent up —— giving such delight?

indicators.note: in a down clue, sending up turns the piece to read bottom to top
the note is placed inside the flowers

parts.note: roses are flowers
N, a note abbreviation as in north or simply 'n'
Y is an unknown in algebra

explanation.surface: A gift of flowers from a secret admirer, with a note tucked in, gives delight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent up' reverses ROSES with N inside (ROSNES) to give SENSOR, then the unknown Y follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Delight of the senses is sensory pleasure, so this adjective describes what such delight comes from.

clue.text: Hateful itch a patient suffers

indicators.note: the words suffer, being knocked into a new shape

explanation.surface: A patient endures an irritating, horrible itch.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipathy is strong dislike, so an antipathetic thing is hostile or hateful.

clue.text: All counties' players: one county not first-class

definitions.meaning: the people employed by each county are their ..., plural of staff
The short form of Staffordshire, an English county without first-class cricket status

explanation.surface: A remark on county cricket squads and one minor county.
explanation.walkthrough: Staffordshire is an English county that plays only minor-county cricket, not the top first-class championship.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: the employees of several bodies, and the standard abbreviation of an English county.

clue.text: Almost commonplace to have single interval

indicators.note: almost all of the word is kept, so its final letter drops away

parts.note: trite means hackneyed, commonplace
one means single

explanation.surface: Something nearly ordinary contains just one interval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' cuts the E from TRITE.
explanation.definitionFit: In music a tritone is the interval of three whole tones, the augmented fourth.

clue.text: Rebel against God prostrated himself, needing a new support to get up

parts.note: one who has thrown himself down has fallen
taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting up turns the word to read upwards

parts.note: a leg is a support, as of a table

explanation.surface: Someone flat on the ground needs a fresh prop to rise again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To get up' reverses LEG to GEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucifer and his followers, cast out of heaven, are the classic example of rebels against God.

clue.text: In hearing, addressed by title? That's irrational

indicators.note: in hearing means the word is judged by how it sounds spoken

parts.note: someone called 'sir' has been sirred

explanation.surface: In a courtroom, a man is addressed as 'sir', which seems unreasonable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearing' suggests a court hearing; it signals a sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: In mathematics a surd is an irrational root, such as the square root of two.

clue.text: Observe a range covered by betting system

indicators.note: the inner pieces are covered, placed inside the outer word

parts.note: the tote is a pool betting system
taken as written
ken is range of knowledge

explanation.surface: Watch a range of odds offered by the bookmakers.
explanation.definitionFit: To take note of something is to notice or observe it.

clue.text: One running round lake, a grinding task for him

indicators.note: the runner goes round the lake, so it sits inside

parts.note: a miler is one who runs the mile

explanation.surface: A jogger circling a lake finds it a gruelling chore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grinding' looks like weariness; it is literal, a mill grinding corn.
explanation.definitionFit: A miller's whole trade is grinding grain into flour.

clue.text: Fine material in oriental pancake?

definitions.meaning: French crêpe 'of China', a pancake from the East read literally

explanation.surface: A dainty fabric appears in an eastern pancake.
explanation.walkthrough: The fabric name is French for 'crêpe of China', and a crêpe is a thin pancake.
explanation.definitionFit: Both readings hold: a fine silk cloth, and literally a pancake from China.

clue.text: Taking off proper suit, change into what's appropriate

indicators.note: to change the words is to rework their letters

explanation.surface: Removing a formal suit and changing into suitable clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking off' reads as undressing; 'off' is fodder and 'change' signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fit for purpose does its job properly, being appropriate.

clue.text: Poet's slow eating almost scalding potato

definitions.note: the poet is: 's is 'is', linking definition and wordplay

indicators.note: the slow word eats the other pieces, holding them inside

parts.note: tardy means slow or late

indicators.note: almost all is kept, the final letter dropped

parts.note: scalding means very hot
mash is mashed potato

explanation.surface: A poet slowly eats a nearly scalding potato.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' removes the last letter of the scalding word before it joins the potato inside the slow one. Hardy wrote poems as well as novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Hardy was a celebrated English poet as well as novelist.

clue.text: Artist lays off woman that refused sex

indicators.note: off means faulty or wrong, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A painter dismisses a woman who would not sleep with him.
explanation.walkthrough: In Aristophanes' comedy Lysistrata leads Greek women in a sex strike to end war.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of the Greek comedy organises women to withhold sex from their husbands.

clue.text: Aerobatic stunt may be deranged

definitions.meaning: a flying stunt full of loops could be called loop-y

explanation.surface: A risky flying manoeuvre might be crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for crazy, and literally full of loops like an aerobatic display.

clue.text: Always crossing river on sort of truck? Far from it — in the air

definitions.text: Far from it — in the air

indicators.note: the always-and-river piece is put on after the truck

parts.note: a tipper is a lorry that tips its load

indicators.note: the always word goes across the river, holding it inside

parts.note: ay is a poetic word for always

explanation.surface: A truck forever crossing a river, though it seems far away.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition recalls the song 'It's a Long Way to Tipperary', so Tipperary is far from 'it' in the tune (the air). Tipperary is an Irish county.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous wartime song says it is a long way to this Irish place.

clue.text: Cuddling boy, chilly in a place of mine

indicators.note: the chilly word cuddles the boy, wrapping round him

parts.note: cold means chilly
Alfie is a boy's name

explanation.surface: Someone hugs a boy who is cold in their own home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Place of mine' looks like 'my place'; it means a place where there are mines.
explanation.definitionFit: A coalfield is an area with coal seams and the pits that work them.

clue.text: Holding pot, stand opposite cooker

indicators.note: the face word holds the pot inside

parts.note: to face is to stand opposite
an urn is a pot or vessel

explanation.surface: Holding a pot, someone stands across from the stove.
explanation.definitionFit: A furnace is an enclosed structure for intense heating, a cooker in a loose sense.

clue.text: Singer's performance likely to stop a short way in

definitions.note: the singer is: 's is 'is', linking the definition

parts.note: a gig is a musical performance

indicators.text: to stop a short way in
indicators.note: the word stops after only a short distance, so only its opening survives

explanation.surface: A singer's concert looks likely to end soon after it starts.
explanation.walkthrough: Beniamino Gigli was a famous Italian tenor.
explanation.definitionFit: Gigli was a celebrated operatic tenor, so a singer.

clue.text: Good to see through what Meldrew does

parts.note: to rumble someone is to see through them

explanation.surface: Good to see through the habits of a famous TV grouch.
explanation.walkthrough: Victor Meldrew is the endlessly complaining hero of the British sitcom One Foot in the Grave.
explanation.definitionFit: The sitcom character is famous for complaining, which is grumbling.

clue.text: Stunning success by brave allowed two lines by Chaucer

indicators.note: by means beside, so the brave word sits next to the rest

parts.note: heroic means brave
a coup is a brilliant success
let means allowed

explanation.surface: A brave poet is credited with a triumph of two lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaucer pioneered the rhyming pair of iambic pentameter lines in English.

clue.text: Fine diary to sell

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencils
a log is a diary or record

explanation.surface: A fine journal for sale.
explanation.walkthrough: To flog is British slang for selling.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal British usage for selling or peddling goods.

clue.text: Tether dog after turn round middle of park

indicators.note: the turned dog goes round the park's middle
the dog word comes after being turned back to front

parts.note: to dog is to tail, follow

indicators.note: only the central letters of the word are used

explanation.surface: Tie up the dog after a walk round the park.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After turn' reads the dog word backwards before it wraps the two central letters of park.
explanation.definitionFit: A lariat is a rope for tethering or lassoing animals.

clue.text: Spy team volunteers to eat club sandwich made with this?

indicators.note: the spy and volunteers take the club inside

parts.note: the CIA is the US spy agency
TA is the Territorial Army, British volunteer reserve
a bat is a club

explanation.surface: A spy team and volunteers eat a club sandwich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club sandwich' is a known phrase; 'club' is BAT and 'sandwich made with this?' defines the bread. 'Team' is padding.
explanation.definitionFit: Ciabatta is an Italian bread often used for making sandwiches.

clue.text: Duck's short drink

indicators.note: short means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: teal is a duck; 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A duck takes a quick drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' cuts TEAL to TEA.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea is a common hot drink.

clue.text: Sound chap, one named Old Faithful

indicators.note: sound means a word heard spoken

parts.note: geezer is British slang for a man, a chap

explanation.surface: A reliable man is nicknamed Old Faithful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound chap' reads as a reliable man; 'Sound' signals the sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Faithful in Yellowstone is the most famous hot spring that erupts.

clue.text: Rum and mead, rare mixture

indicators.note: a mixture of the words gives their letters jumbled

explanation.surface: Rum and mead mixed together are rarely seen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the drink; it is, Demerara rum from Guyana.
explanation.definitionFit: Demerara is a dark rum from Guyana.
